extracted.intended_audience: newspaper editors, professional journalists, and students of journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and professional standards for producing and running a modern newspaper — reporting, editorial policy, staffing, training, business practice, and the ethical/political role of the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the news
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the news, get all the news, and nothing but the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News is defined broadly as 'everything that occurs, everything which is of human interest and which is of sufficient importance to arrest and absorb the attention of the public or of any considerable part of it.' Prioritize gathering comprehensive, relevant information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy nothing from another publication without perfect credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never present another publication's material as your own. Always give full, explicit credit when using content from other outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Never print an interview without the knowledge and consent of the party interviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain explicit permission before publishing interviews; respect interviewees' rights and avoid covert or surreptitious publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate advertising from news
rubrics_metrics.description: Never print a paid advertisement as news matter. Let every advertisement appear as an advertisement; no sailing under false colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear labeling and separation between editorial content and paid material to preserve reader trust and editorial integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attacking the weak or defenseless
rubrics_metrics.description: Never attack the weak or the defenseless, either by argument, by invective, or by ridicule, unless there is some absolute public necessity for so doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint and ethical judgment before using the paper's power to criticize; attacks should be reserved for matters of clear public necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Fight for your opinions, but do not believe that they contain the whole truth or the only truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remain partisan or advocative where appropriate, but retain humility and openness to other perspectives; avoid claiming exclusive moral or factual authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party loyalty with balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Support your party, if you have one. But do not think all the good men are in it and all the bad ones outside of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow party alignment to inform stance but not to blind judgement; recognize virtues and faults across political lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimism about progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Above all, know and believe that humanity is advancing; that there is progress in human life and human affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an editorial outlook that recognizes progress and improvement over time; this principle should inform tone and long-term perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found newspaper on human nature and audience needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper must be founded upon human nature. It must correspond to the wants of the people. It must furnish that sort of information which the people demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know your readership's interests, feelings, and needs; tailor content to serve and reflect the community while maintaining professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish matters of public interest without undue limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper should publish events and matters of human interest; the author resists proposals to limit certain kinds of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution before excluding news categories; err on informing readers about events 'Providence permitted to occur' unless there is a compelling reason to withhold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and bear the press's power and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The press shapes opinion—sometimes suggesting judgments before individuals form them—and thus has a solemn responsibility. It can speak the voice of justice and be a bulwark against tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should appreciate the influence of their pages, avoid misleading or manipulative uses of that influence, and use the press to defend constitutional liberties and public welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal education for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper man must be an all-around man; his education should be exceedingly extensive — college studies plus practical life experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage broad general education (including classical languages where possible) so journalists can judge theological, medical, legal, scientific, artistic questions with informed competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical newsroom apprenticeship
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper office is the best post-graduate college for a journalist; practical work in an office is indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement formal education with hands-on training in a working newspaper; on-the-job learning and mentorship by experienced editors are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the critical faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the judgment which sees truth when presented and detects error without long examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train reporters and editors to think critically, to evaluate claims swiftly and accurately, and not to be taken in by plausible falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and fidelity in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy — seeing a thing as it is and reporting the fact just as it is — is one of the first and most precious ends of a good education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize factual precision, measurements, and exactness across all reporting (from sports to science); do not exaggerate or misstate facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of expression — tell what you know
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to tell what you know; the ability to state facts accurately and clearly is central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate concise, precise written and spoken expression so readers understand facts and arguments without confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make truth interesting — vivid presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The invariable law of the newspaper is to be interesting. Truth told tediously fails to reach readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present facts vividly and engagingly: lively prose, narrative color, and human interest enhance retention and impact; balance readability with accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business education for journalists and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper men require a business education and personal knowledge of business methods; practical business contact is invaluable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure newsroom leaders understand economics, advertising, circulation, production costs, and commercial realities that affect editorial decisions and paper viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never be in a hurry
rubrics_metrics.description: Never be in a hurry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise editorial patience: verify facts, check sources, avoid rushed judgments that lead to errors or ethical lapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand by constitutional principles and liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold fast to the Constitution. Stand by the Stars and Stripes. Above all, stand for Liberty, whatever happens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the newspaper's mission as protective of constitutional liberties and republican forms; use editorial voice to defend fundamental rights and democratic institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit errors and avoid feigned infallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find you have been wrong, don't fear to say so. There is a tradition that pretends to silly infallibility; that is a silly rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish corrections and retractions openly; value moral courage over pride. Transparency about mistakes preserves credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize staff with defined roles and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: A modern newspaper needs a trained staff of reporters, correspondents, editorial writers (by subject), exchange reader, city editor, managing editor, and a business manager.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff the paper with specialists: subject-matter editorialists, bureaus/correspondents for geography, an exchange reader to curate external coverage, a city editor to manage local reporting, and managing/editorial leaders to coordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A good reporter must 'know the truth when he hears it and sees it' and be able to state the fact in a clear, vivid, and interesting manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hire reporters with truth-detection instincts, observational skill, accuracy, energetically vivid prose, and the ability to feel and convey the story's qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of the exchange reader/curator
rubrics_metrics.description: The exchange reader (newspaper reader) who scans and extracts valuable items from other papers is very important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designate staff for monitoring other publications and curating content to ensure broad, timely coverage and to incorporate valuable external reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in visual art and illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sunday pictures and other illustrations are costly but important; skilled artists (often women for fashion drawings) can command steady pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate meaningful budget for high-quality artwork and photography; visuals increase reader engagement and can be a differentiator in competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics, scale, and circulation matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern printing machinery, broad distribution, and large circulation enable the 'modern newspaper' and underpin its intellectual and commercial operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision adequate printing technology, distribution networks, and circulation strategies to reach the intended audience; consider economies of scale in major markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use promotional circulation strategically (ethical cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Printing and distributing free or promotional copies can increase apparent circulation and attract advertisers, but this practice can be gamed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ promotional distribution to demonstrate reach to advertisers but maintain truthful accounting of paid vs. promotional circulation and avoid deceptive inflation of figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring and advancement by merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Young staff are typically promoted from the bottom up in accordance with faculties and merits; offices should aim to develop talent internally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create apprenticeship pathways, evaluate staff by demonstrated ability in daily competition and performance, and promote based on merit rather than favoritism.
